inline.s: But since the serpent of the mind-only has already appeared, it is able to bite; since the money of the mind-only has already appeared, it is available to be enjoyed. If it were not mind-only, there would be no external world at all. Moreover, the defiled suffering of the Sahā world and the pure bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss are likewise both manifested by the mind alone. Since the defiled suffering of the mind-only has appeared, one undergoes great oppression; since the pure bliss of the mind-only has appeared, one enjoys great benefit. Since both defiled suffering and pure bliss are manifested by the mind alone, why not abandon the defiled suffering of the mind-only and take up the pure bliss of the mind-only, yet still deliberately endure the torment of the Eight Sufferings through long kalpas!

[The Eight Sufferings] The suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of sickness, the suffering of death, the suffering of separation from what one loves, the suffering of meeting with what one hates, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the blazing of the five aggregates.

blocks.text: 13. The Power of the Mind and the Power of Karma

inline.s: The power of the mind and the power of karma: At the critical juncture of birth and death, there are but two powers — the power of the mind and the power of karma. The power of karma is the greatest, yet the power of the mind is even greater. A person who recites the Buddha's name must make the power of the mind greater than the power of karma before he can bring about the Buddha's appearance to receive and guide him.

[At the critical juncture of birth and death, there are but two powers. The first: thoughts are many and various, and where the mind leans most heavily it falls — this is the power of the mind. The second: as a man in debt is seized first by his strongest creditor, so among the many karma the strongest draws one onward — this is the power of karma. The power of karma is the greatest, yet the power of the mind is even greater. Because karma has no self-nature and relies entirely upon the mind; the mind can create karma and the mind can turn karma. Therefore only when the power of the mind is concentrated and the power of karma is strong can they pull one into rebirth. If with a concentrated mind one cultivates the pure karma, then the pure karma becomes strong; with the mind weighed down and the karma strong, one heads only for the Western Land. Thus when one's life comes to an end at death, one will certainly be reborn in the Western Land and nowhere else. Like a great tree or a great wall that has leaned westward all along — if it falls some day, it will never fall in any other direction.]

At the critical juncture of birth and death, only two powers are at work. The first: thoughts are many and various, and at the moment of rebirth whichever thought weighs most heavily goes to the place that corresponds to it — this is the working of the power of the mind. The second: as a man in debt repays first the greatest debt, so among the many karma at the moment of rebirth whichever karma is strongest goes to the place corresponding to it — this is the working of the power of karma. The power of karma is the greatest, yet the power of the mind is even greater. This is because karma has no self-nature and relies entirely upon the mind. The mind can create karma, and the mind can also turn karma. Therefore the power of the mind pushes the consciousness toward where the thoughts weigh most heavily, while the power of karma pushes the consciousness toward where the karma is strongest; both together determine the place of rebirth. If with a heavy, concentrated mind one cultivates the pure karma, then the pure karma is strong; and with the mind heavy upon rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and the pure karma strong, both the power of the mind and the power of karma push the consciousness toward the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Thus when one's life comes to an end, the consciousness will certainly be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss and nowhere else. This is like a great tree or a great wall, which normally leans westward; if it falls some day, it will only fall to the west.

[What is a concentrated mind? We who cultivate the pure karma treasure faith above depth and vows above earnestness. Because faith is deep and vows are earnest, no false doctrine can shake or confuse, and no circumstance or condition can lure or turn us. If while earnestly cultivating the pure karma Bodhidharma the Great Master should suddenly appear before us and say: “I have the Chan of directly pointing to the human mind, seeing the nature, and becoming Buddha. You have only to set aside Buddha-recitation, and I shall transmit this Chan to you,” we should simply bow to the patriarch and reply: “I have already received the Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation from Sakyamuni Tathagata and have vowed to uphold it my whole life without change. Although the patriarch has a profound and subtle Chan teaching, I dare not violate my own original vow.” Even if Sakyamuni Tathagata were suddenly to appear and say: “What I earlier taught as the Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation was merely an expedient for that time. Now there is a yet more supreme Dharma-door surpassing it. You should set aside Buddha-recitation for now and I shall teach you the supreme Dharma,” we should likewise bow to the Buddha and declare: “I have already received the World-Honored One's Dharma-door of pure karma and have vowed, so long as a single breath remains, never to change. Although the Tathagata has a supreme Dharma, I dare not violate my own original vow.” Even when the Buddha and the patriarchs appear in person, one does not change his faith; how much less can the false, deluded doctrines of Mara and the heterodox teachers shake or confuse it! To have faith like this may indeed be called deep faith.]

So then, what is a concentrated mind? We who cultivate the pure karma treasure faith above depth and vows above earnestness, and because faith is deep and vows are earnest, no false doctrine can confuse or shake us, and no circumstance or condition can lure or turn us. If while earnestly cultivating the pure karma Bodhidharma the Great Master should suddenly appear before us and say: “I have the Chan of directly pointing to the human mind, seeing the nature, and becoming Buddha. You have only to give up Buddha-recitation and I shall transmit this Chan to you,” we should simply bow to the patriarch and answer: “I have already received the Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation from Sakyamuni Tathagata and have vowed to uphold it my whole life without change. Although the patriarch has a profound and subtle Chan teaching, I dare not violate my own original vow.” Even if Sakyamuni Tathagata were suddenly to appear and say: “What I earlier spoke as the Dharma-door of Buddha-recitation was merely an expedient for a time. Now I have a yet more supreme Dharma-door surpassing Buddha-recitation. You have only to give up Buddha-recitation and I shall teach you the supreme Dharma,” we should likewise bow to the Buddha and report: “I have already received the World-Honored One's Dharma-door of pure karma and have vowed, so long as a single breath remains, never to change. Although the Tathagata has a supreme Dharma, I dare not violate my own original vow.” Even when the Buddha and the patriarchs appear and still do not change what one believes, how much less can Mara and the heterodox teachers, with their false, deluded doctrines, confuse or shake one! To have faith like this may be spoken of as deep faith.

[If a red-hot iron wheel were spinning above one's head, one would not, because of this suffering, retreat from the vow to be reborn. If the supreme, wonderful five desires of a wheel-turning king appeared before one, one would not, because of this bliss, retreat from the vow to be reborn. These are the extremes of adversity and prosperity, and yet they do not change one's vow — how much less could the trivial favorable and adverse circumstances of the world lure one away! To have a vow like this may indeed be called an earnest vow.]

If a red-hot iron wheel were spinning above one's head, one would not, because of the menace of this suffering, retreat from the vow to be reborn. If the supreme, wonderful five desires of a wheel-turning king appeared before one, one would not, because of the allure of this bliss, retreat from the vow to be reborn. These extreme adverse and favorable circumstances still cannot change one's vow — how much less could the trivial favorable and adverse circumstances of the world lure and turn one! To have a vow like this may be spoken of as an earnest vow.

[Deep faith and earnest vows are what is called a concentrated mind. Cultivating the pure karma with these, the pure karma is certain to be strong. Because the mind is concentrated it easily becomes pure; because the karma is strong it easily ripens. If the pure karma of the Land of Ultimate Bliss ripens, then the defiled conditions of the Sahā world are exhausted. If the defiled conditions are truly exhausted, then at the moment of death, even if one wished the realms of samsara to appear again, they cannot. If the pure karma has truly ripened, then at the moment of death, even if one wished the Pure Land of Amitabha not to appear, it cannot.]

Deep faith and earnest vows — this is what is called a concentrated mind. Cultivating the pure karma with them, the pure karma is certain to be strong. Because the mind is concentrated it easily becomes single and pure; because the karma is strong the karma easily ripens. If the pure karma of the Land of Ultimate Bliss ripens, then the defiled conditions of the Sahā world are exhausted. If the defiled conditions are truly exhausted, then at the moment of death, even if one wished the realms of samsara to appear again, they cannot. If the pure karma has truly ripened, then at the moment of death, even if one wished the Pure Land of Amitabha not to appear, it cannot.

[But this faith and vow must be maintained with constant practice through ordinary days, so that at the final moment one will not enter a wrong path. There was an ancient worthy who, as he was about to die, was received in succession by the young attendants of the Six Desire Heavens, yet he went with none of them, only fixing his mind upon awaiting the Buddha. When the Buddha later appeared, he said: “The Buddha has come,” and with hands joined he passed away. Now at the very moment of death, when the four elements are dissolving, what a time that is! When the heavenly attendants of the Six Desire Heavens come to receive one after another, what a state that is! If one's faith and vow have not reached complete firmness in ordinary days, when facing such a time and such a state, could one still forcibly maintain mastery? An ancient worthy like this may truly be called a model for all who cultivate the pure karma through the ages.]

And yet such deep faith and earnest vows must be maintained with constant practice through ordinary days, so that at the final moment one will naturally not enter a wrong path. For example, an ancient worthy, as he was about to die, was received in succession by the heavenly attendants of the Six Desire Heavens, yet he went with none of them, only fixing his mind upon awaiting the arrival of Amitabha Buddha. Only when Amitabha Buddha appeared before him did he say: “The Buddha has come,” and with hands joined he passed away. Now at the moment of death, when the four elements dissolve, what a time that is! When the heavenly attendants of the Six Desire Heavens come to receive one after another, what a state that is! If in ordinary days one's faith and vow have not reached complete firmness, when facing such a time and such a state, where could one forcibly maintain mastery? An ancient worthy like this may truly be called a model for all who cultivate the pure karma through the ages.

blocks.text: 14. Practicing the Way Within the Dream

inline.s: Practicing the Way within the dream: use the illusory to depart from the illusory; when illusion is exhausted, the dream awakens.

[A Chan practitioner once asked: “All dharmas are like a dream. The Sahā world is indeed a dream, and the Land of Ultimate Bliss is also a dream. Since both are dreams, what benefit is there in practicing?”

A Chan practitioner asked: “All dharmas are like a dream. The Sahā world is indeed a dream, and the Land of Ultimate Bliss is also a dream. Since both are dreams, what benefit is there in cultivating within the dream?”

[I replied: “Not so. Before the seventh ground, one practices the Way within a dream. The great dream of ignorance is one from which even an equal-enlightenment bodhisattva still sleeps. Only the Buddha alone may be called the Great Awakened One. While the eye of the dream has not yet opened, suffering and bliss appear quite real. Better than dreaming of the extreme suffering of the Sahā world is dreaming of the wonderful bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Moreover, the dream of the Sahā world goes from dream into deeper dream — dream upon dream, sinking ever more deeply. The dream of the Land of Ultimate Bliss goes from dream into awakening — awakening upon awakening, gradually reaching the Great Awakening. Although both are dreams, the one who dreams them is not the same; how can they be discussed as one?”

I replied: “You are mistaken. Before the seventh ground, bodhisattvas all practice the Way within a dream. The great dream of ignorance is one from which even an equal-enlightenment bodhisattva has not fully awakened. Only the Buddha alone may be called completely awake (the Great Awakening). While the eye of the dream has not yet opened, the suffering and bliss within the dream appear quite real. Better than dreaming of the extreme suffering of the Sahā world is dreaming of the wonderful bliss of the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Moreover, the dream of the Sahā world goes from dream into deeper dream — dream upon dream, ever more lost. The dream of the Land of Ultimate Bliss goes from dream into awakening — awakening upon awakening, gradually becoming completely awake. Although the Sahā world and the Land of Ultimate Bliss are both dreams, the nature of the two dreams is utterly different; how can they be lumped together?”
Faith is especially essential: in the great ocean of the Buddha-Dharma, faith is what allows entrance. In the single gate of the Pure Land, faith is especially essential.

[In the great ocean of the Buddha-Dharma, faith is what allows entrance. In the single gate of the Pure Land, faith is especially essential. Because the recitation of the Buddha's name is the profound practice-ground of all the Buddhas. Except for the bodhisattva bound for Buddhahood in one lifetime, who may know a small portion of it, all the other sages and worthies can only follow it in faith — it is not within the reach of their wisdom, how much less that of inferior common mortals!]

In the great ocean of the Buddha-Dharma, only faith allows entrance. In the Pure Land Dharma-door, faith is all the more essential. Because the recitation of the Buddha's name is the profound practice-ground of all the Buddhas. Except for the equal-enlightenment bodhisattva, who knows a portion of it, all the other sages and worthies should only follow it in deep faith — for its principle is not within the reach of their wisdom, how much less that of inferior common mortals!

[Bodhisattva bound for Buddhahood in one lifetime] That is, the bodhisattva of one more rebirth — the equal-enlightenment bodhisattva — who, at the end of this very life, is able to fill the Buddha's seat.

[Moreover, of the eleven wholesome dharmas, faith occupies the first place; before faith there is no other wholesome dharma. Of the fifty-two stages, faith is the beginning; before the stage of faith there is no other sage-stage. Therefore the bodhisattva composed the Awakening of Faith, and the patriarch wrote the Inscription on Faith — taking the single dharma of faith as the essential gate for entering the Way. In former times Wang Zhonghui asked Yang Wuwei: “How can one's Buddha-recitation become uninterrupted?” Yang replied: “After a single moment of faith, one no longer doubts.” Wang departed joyfully. Before long, Yang dreamed that Zhonghui came to thank him, saying: “Through your instruction I gained great benefit, and I have now been reborn in the Pure Land.” Yang later met Zhonghui's son and asked about the circumstances of Zhonghui's passing and the time of it — which turned out to be the very day Yang had the dream. Alas! How great is the meaning of the moment of faith!]

Moreover, of the eleven wholesome mental factors, faith occupies the first place; before faith there is no other wholesome dharma. Of the fifty-two stages, faith is the beginning; before the stage of faith there is no other sage-stage. Therefore the bodhisattva Asvaghosa composed the Awakening of Faith, and the Third Patriarch of the Chan school, Sengcan, wrote the Inscription on Faith — each taking the single dharma of faith as the essential gate for entering the Way. In former times Wang Zhonghui asked Yang Wuwei: “How can one's Buddha-recitation become uninterrupted?” Yang Wuwei replied: “After a single moment of faith, one no longer doubts.” Wang Zhonghui departed joyfully. Before long, Yang Wuwei dreamed that Zhonghui came to thank him, saying: “Through your instruction I gained great benefit, and I have now been reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.” Yang Wuwei later met Zhonghui's son and asked about the circumstances and the time of Zhonghui's passing — which turned out to be the very day Yang Wuwei had the dream. Alas! How important faith is!

[The Eleven Wholesome Dharmas] That is, the eleven wholesome mental factors, one of the six groups of mental factors established by the Consciousness-Only school, namely: faith, shame, dread of blame, absence of greed, absence of anger, absence of delusion, diligence, tranquility, non-laxity, equanimity in relinquishment, and non-harmfulness. [Mental Factors] An abbreviation for the dharmas belonging to the mind — the various mental phenomena that belong to the mind, fifty-one in all. [Fifty-Two Stages] The stages a bodhisattva passes through from a common mortal to Buddhahood, fifty-two in all: the ten faiths, the ten abodes, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment. [Yang Wuwei] Yang Jie, style name Cigong, a man of Wuwei in Jiangsu, who called himself “Master Wuwei.” During the Yuanfeng era of Emperor Shenzong of the Northern Song, he held the office of “Taichang”
in charge of the affairs of ritual, music, the suburban temples, and the altars of soil and grain

. After his great awakening, he turned his heart to the Pure Land. He wrote the Preface to the Ten Doubts of the Tiantai School, the Record of the Amitabha Pavilion, Thirty Hymns in Praise of the Land of Peace and Nurture, and the Preface to the Collection Resolving Doubts on the Pure Land, widely proclaiming the contemplation doctrines of the Western Land to guide those of future ages. In his later years he painted an image of Amitabha Buddha and carried it with him for contemplation and recollection. On the day of his death, his sincerity brought the Buddha to welcome him, and he passed away seated upright.

[The monk Dharmakara, before the Buddha World-Self-Ruling King, made forty-eight great vows in accordance with his nature. Relying upon these vows, through countless long kalpas he cultivated the great practices, until cause was complete and fruit fulfilled, and he himself became a Buddha. Dharmakara's name changed to Amitabha, and the world changed to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. What makes Amitabha Amitabha is that he has deeply realized the mind-only self-nature. Yet are not this Amitabha and this Land of Ultimate Bliss the mind-only Amitabha and the mind-only Land of Ultimate Bliss of the self-nature? But this mind-nature is equally shared by living beings and Buddhas; it belongs not particularly to the Buddha, nor particularly to living beings.]

The monk Dharmakara, before the Buddha World-Self-Ruling King, made forty-eight great vows in accordance with his nature. Relying upon these forty-eight great vows, through countless long kalpas he cultivated the great practices, until cause was complete and fruit fulfilled and he became a Buddha. At that time Dharmakara's name changed to Amitabha Buddha, and the world changed to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. What makes Amitabha Buddha Amitabha Buddha is that he has deeply realized the mind-only self-nature. Yet is not this Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitabha Buddha the mind-only Land of Ultimate Bliss of the self-nature Amita? But this mind-nature is equally shared by living beings and Buddhas; it belongs not particularly to a Buddha, nor particularly to living beings.
[The monk Dharmakara] The name of Amitabha Buddha when, in the causal stage, he left home before the Buddha World-Self-Ruling King and practiced the bodhisattva path.

[If one attributes the mind to Amitabha, then living beings are the living beings within Amitabha's mind. If one attributes the mind to living beings, then Amitabha is the Amitabha within living beings' minds. When the living being within Amitabha's mind recites the Amitabha within the living being's mind, how could the Amitabha within the living being's mind not respond to the living being within Amitabha's mind?]

If one attributes the mind to Amitabha Buddha, then living beings are the living beings within Amitabha Buddha's mind. If one attributes the mind to living beings, then Amitabha Buddha is the Amitabha Buddha within living beings' minds. When the living being within Amitabha Buddha's mind recites the Amitabha Buddha within the living being's mind, how could the Amitabha Buddha within the living being's mind not respond to the living being within Amitabha Buddha's mind?

[But the Buddha, awakened to this mind, is like a man who is awake. Living beings, deluded about this mind, are like men in a dream. Apart from the man who is awake, there is no other man in the dream. How could there be, apart from the man in the dream, another man who is awake? But the man in the dream should not take himself to be real, nor should he, apart from the man in the dream, seek another man who is awake; he should only ever remember the man who is awake. Remembering again and again, he will see the great dream gradually awaken and the eye of the dream open wide. Then the man in the dream who is able to remember is the very man who is awake whom he remembers. But the man who is awake is not the man in the dream. The men in the dream are many; the man who is awake is only one. The Tathagatas of the ten directions share one single dharmakaya; one mind, one wisdom, and likewise the powers and the fearlessnesses. This is the Dharma of at once one and many, ever the same and ever distinct, naturally and spontaneously wonderful. The essential meaning of Buddha-recitation is roughly this.]

But the Buddha, awakened to this mind, is like a man who is awake; living beings, deluded about this mind, are like men in a dream. Apart from the man who is awake, there is no other man in the dream. Apart from the man in the dream, how could there be another man who is awake? But the man in the dream should not take the affairs of the dream to be real, nor should he, apart from the man in the dream, seek another man who is awake; he should only always remember the man who is awake (the Buddha). Remembering again and again, he will see the great dream gradually awaken and the eye of the dream open wide. Then the man in the dream who is able to remember is the very man who is awake whom he remembers. But the man who is awake is not the man in the dream. The men in the dream are many; the man who is awake is only one. The Tathagatas of the ten directions share one single dharmakaya; one mind, one wisdom, and likewise the powers and the fearlessnesses. This is the Dharma of at once one and many, ever the same and ever distinct, naturally and spontaneously wonderful. The essential meaning of Buddha-recitation is roughly this.

blocks.text: 17. The Perfect Interfusion of Phenomenon and Principle

inline.s: The perfect interfusion of phenomenon and principle: “Reborn — one is certainly reborn; gone — one truly does not go.”

[The two statements “Reborn — one is certainly reborn; gone — one truly does not go” are held to speak: the first of phenomenon, the second of principle. Phenomenon is phenomenon that is identical to principle, meaning that to be born is not to be born — not that birth is taken simply as birth. Principle is principle that is identical to phenomenon, meaning that not to go is to go — not that not-going is taken simply as not-going. Read the two statements as one, then phenomenon and principle are perfectly interfused, so that joined they are doubly beautiful. Read the two statements as two, then phenomenon and principle are split apart, so that separated they are doubly injured. If one does not join these two statements as one, one should expand them into four statements: Reborn — one is certainly reborn, yet born without birth; gone — one truly does not go, yet not-going is to go.]

Reborn — one is certainly reborn; gone — one truly does not go,” these two sentences: the first speaks of phenomenon, the second speaks of principle. Phenomenon does not depart from principle — the “birth” of “reborn — one is certainly reborn” is non-birth, not taking birth simply as birth. Principle does not depart from phenomenon — the “not going” of “gone — one truly does not go” is going, not taking not-going simply as not-going. Read the two sentences as one, then phenomenon and principle are perfectly interfused — the so-called joined, doubly beautiful. Read the two sentences as two, then phenomenon and principle are split apart — the so-called separated, doubly injured. If one does not join these two sentences as one, one should expand these two sentences into four: Reborn — one is certainly reborn, yet born without birth; gone — one truly does not go, yet not-going is to go.

The Diamond Sutra says: “All conditioned appearances are false and unreal.” Rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is an affair within the dream of ignorance, so it too is an illusion. The characteristic of an illusion is that the appearance exists while the essence is non-existent — that is, the phenomenon exists while the principle is non-existent. The passage “Reborn — one is certainly reborn; gone — one truly does not go” speaks of rebirth from the two aspects of phenomenon and principle. From the aspect of phenomenal appearance, “reborn — one is certainly reborn” — one truly is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; from the aspect of principle, “gone — one truly does not go” — in reality there is no such affair as going to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore the passage “Reborn — one is certainly reborn; gone — one truly does not go” must be read as one sentence, speaking of the two aspects of phenomenon and principle. If read as two sentences, they become two mutually contradictory and confusing statements. So if not read as one sentence, one should expand them into four: Reborn — one is certainly reborn, yet born without birth (birth is illusion; in reality one was not born); gone — one truly does not go, yet not-going is to go (though on the essential principle one does not go, on the phenomenal appearance one goes).

In this book, Master Chewu often explains the principles of the Pure Land from the standpoint of the true reality of all dharmas, so it is best to read it after completing the four courses — the Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra, the Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra, the Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, and the Selected Annotations on the Buddha-Treasure Sutra — in the stage of “Prajna that Destroys Delusion” of “Practicing Accordingly,” and it will then be easy to understand.

[Though they be four statements, the meaning is no more; joined as one statement, the meaning is no less. All in all it is just the perfect interfusion of phenomenon and principle. Rather than cling to the principle of “gone — one truly does not go,” it is better to cling to the phenomenon of “reborn — one is certainly reborn.” Why? Because clinging to phenomenon while being blind to principle still does not fail to gain the merit of entering a grade. But if one clings to principle and abandons phenomenon, one inevitably incurs the reproach of falling into emptiness. This is because phenomenon has the power to accord with principle, while principle has no power to stand alone. To take birth as birth is to fall into the eternalist view; to take not-going as not-going (denying even the phenomenal appearance) is to fall into the nihilist view. Though nihilism and eternalism are equally wrong views, the fault of the nihilist view is the deeper and heavier, and so it is better to cling to phenomenon. Yet after all, nothing is better than to perfectly comprehend the two statements together.]

“Reborn — one is certainly reborn, yet born without birth; gone — one truly does not go, yet not-going is to go,” though they be four statements, the meaning is not increased. Joined as one statement, the meaning is not decreased. Whether four statements or one, all are but bringing about the perfect interfusion of phenomenon and principle. If one cannot achieve this perfect interfusion, then rather than cling to the principle of “gone — one truly does not go,” it is better to cling to the phenomenon of “reborn — one is certainly reborn.” Why? Because clinging to phenomenon while not understanding principle still has the effect of rebirth in the Pure Land. But if one clings to principle and abandons phenomenon, one inevitably incurs the reproach of falling into emptiness and cannot be reborn in the Pure Land. This is because phenomenon originally contains principle within it — only this person does not understand; while principle can never stand apart from phenomenon — principle without phenomenon is empty talk and fallacious theory. If one thinks of birth as birth, one falls into the eternalist view; if one thinks of not-going as absolute not-going (denying even the phenomenal appearance), one falls into the nihilist view. Though nihilism and eternalism are equally wrong views, nevertheless the fault of nihilism is deep and heavy, and so it is better to cling to phenomenon as having effect. Of course, although practicing by clinging to phenomenon has effect, it is still not as good as perfectly comprehending, from both phenomenon and principle, the two statements “Reborn — one is certainly reborn; gone — one truly does not go.” (Because one who clings to phenomenon without understanding principle may be reborn, but the grade is not high; one who clings to phenomenon yet understands principle — comprehending the first meaning — is reborn in the highest grade.)

blocks.text: 18. The Single Thought at the Moment of Death

inline.s: The single thought at the moment of death: the thousand recitations and the ten thousand recitations, even the day-long and year-long recitation — all are for nothing but to ripen this single thought of Buddha-recitation, in order to ensure that this thought appears at the moment of death.

[Our present single thought is dependently arisen and without self-nature; without self-nature yet dependently arisen. If it is not born in the Buddha-realm, then it is born in the nine realms. From the standpoint of dependent arising without self-nature, living beings and Buddhas are equally one emptiness. From the standpoint of no self-nature yet dependent arising, the ten realms differ vastly in superiority and inferiority.]

Our present single thought arises from causes and conditions and has no self-nature (it is an illusion); though without self-nature, it nonetheless arises following causes and conditions. If it is not born in the Buddha-dharmarealm, then it is born in the nine dharmarealms. From the standpoint of dependent arising without self-nature, living beings and Buddhas are equal, all being one emptiness. From the standpoint of no self-nature yet dependent arising, within the ten dharmarealms the superiority or inferiority of each is vastly disproportionate.

[No self-nature] “No self-nature” means that there is no real substance — it is an illusion, like the affairs of a dream. The Lotus Sutra says: “Know that all dharmas are ever without self-nature.” The Surangama Sutra says: “All illusions become without self-nature.”

[When King Ajitavati was dying, because a servant brushing away flies brushed his face with a whisk, a single thought of anger arose, and because of this he fell and became a poisonous snake. A woman, crossing a river, lost her footing; her child fell into the water, and in rescuing the child she sank with him. Because of her compassionate thought, she was reborn in heaven. When a single thought of compassion or anger thus divides heaven from the animal realm, how can this dependently arisen single thought at death be anything but a matter for care? If with this thought one turns the mind to recite Amitabha and seek rebirth in the Pure Land, how could one fail to see the Buddha and be reborn?]

When King Ajitavati was dying, because the servant brushing away flies carelessly brushed his face with a fan, a single thought of anger arose, and because this dying thought was one of anger, he fell and became a poisonous snake. A woman, crossing a river, lost her footing; her child fell into the water, and because she retrieved the child, both she and the child were submerged. Because her dying thought was one of compassion, this woman was reborn in heaven. When the dying thought is compassion or anger, the compassionate one is born in heaven and the angry one is born among animals — this distinction follows. How can one not be careful with this dependently arisen single thought at death? If at death, with this thought, one turns the mind to recite Amitabha Buddha and seek rebirth in the Pure Land, how could one fail to see the Buddha and be reborn?

[No self-nature] The meaning of “all dharmas are without self-nature” is that all dharmas have no real substance, all being illusions, like the affairs of a dream. No self-nature is also called no-nature. The Consciousness-Only Treatise says: “All dharmas are without self-nature.” The Lotus Sutra says: “Know that all dharmas are ever without self-nature.” The Surangama Sutra says: “All illusions become without self-nature.” [King Ajitavati] That is, King Ajitashatru, who throughout his life built countless stupas, made offerings to the Three Jewels, upheld the true Dharma, and accumulated vast merit. At death, because his attendant carelessly brushed his face with a fan, anger arose, and he fell and became a poisonous snake. This matter is found in the Miscellaneous Similes Sutra.
[The dependently arisen single thought at death] The single thought, at the moment of death, that determines where the consciousness is reborn.

[But this single thought cannot be gained through luck. It must be preserved with sincerity and maintained with constant practice. Therefore we, in this single “Amitabha,” recite a thousand times and ten thousand times, even day-long and year-long — all for nothing but to ripen this single thought. If this single thought ripens to purity, then at the moment of death there is only this thought and no other. Master Zhiyi says: “The mind in concentration at death is the mind that receives rebirth in the Pure Land.” Now when there is only this one thought and no other, is this not the mind in concentration? If the thought is thus, then not seeing Amitabha, whom else would he see? Not being reborn in the Pure Land, where else would he be reborn? I fear only that we do not have confidence in ourselves.]

But this single thought at death cannot be gained through luck. It must be preserved with sincerity and maintained with constant practice. Therefore we, in this single “Amitabha Buddha,” recite a thousand times and ten thousand times, even day-long and year-long — all for nothing but to ripen this single thought of Buddha-recitation, in order to ensure that the thought at death is a thought of Amitabha Buddha. If this single thought of Buddha-recitation ripens to purity, then at the moment of death there is only this thought of Buddha-recitation and no other. Master Zhiyi says: “The mind in concentration at death is the mind that receives rebirth in the Pure Land.” Now when there is only the thought of Buddha-recitation and no other thought, is this not the mind in concentration? Since at death it is the mind in concentration, then not seeing Amitabha Buddha, whom else would he see? Not being reborn in the Pure Land, where else would he be reborn? I fear only that we have not truly believed in the above principle; if we truly believed, how could we not be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss?

[Ripening this single thought] This means achieving what the bodhisattva Mahasthamaprapta called “pure thoughts continuing without interruption,” which is what Master Shandao (the second patriarch of the Pure Land school) called “thought after thought continuous.” (Note: “thought after thought continuous” means that each thought of Buddha-recitation continues into the next; it does not mean the condition of mouthing the Buddha's name while the mind is given over to delusive thinking.) Master Shandao says: “Therefore the Great Sage (Sakyamuni Buddha), in his compassion and pity, directly urged single-minded recitation of the name; precisely because reciting the name is easy, when it is continuous one is reborn. If one can make thought after thought continuous, making the end of life the term, then ten in ten are reborn, a hundred in a hundred are reborn. … If all people will earnestly reflect, then whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying, they must be diligent and strict with themselves, never ceasing by day or night — the former thought ends with life, the latter thought is born, ever enjoying the Dharma-bliss of the unconditioned, even reaching Buddhahood. Is this not blessed?” (Quoted from The Essentials of Buddha-Recitation.) Therefore, thought after thought continuous in daily life is the guarantee of right mindfulness clearly present at death; and right mindfulness clearly present at death is the key to rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Master Shandao composed the Essay on Right Mindfulness at Death, saying: “The one who knows the return asked: Of the great affairs of the world, none surpasses birth and death. When one breath does not come, one belongs to the next life; a single mistaken thought and one falls into samsara. I have repeatedly received your instruction on the Dharma of rebirth through Buddha-recitation, and its principle is most clear. Yet I fear that when sickness comes and death arrives, my mind and consciousness may be scattered, and I still worry that others may disturb my right mindfulness and cause me to lose the pure cause. I humbly beg you to again make clear the path of return, so that I may escape the suffering of sinking. The master said: Good is your question! All people, when about to die, who wish to be reborn in the Pure Land must not fear death. Always think that this body is full of suffering and that impure evil karma entangles it in many ways. If one can abandon this defiled body and be reborn beyond in the Pure Land, receiving immeasurable bliss and being liberated from the bitter realm of birth and death, that is a most satisfying matter — like casting off a worn garment and receiving a precious robe. One should only let go of body and mind and give rise to no attachment. … When illness is grave and death approaches, relatives must not weep in tears or utter sighs of regret and distress, disturbing the mind and confusing the spirit and losing right mindfulness. They should only recite the Buddha's name in unison, and only after the breath has ceased may they grieve and weep. If there is the slightest thought of attachment to the world, it becomes a hindrance and one cannot be liberated. … I have often seen people in the world who in daily life recite, praise, and make vows to seek rebirth in the West with great diligence and sincerity. Yet when sickness comes, they fear death and speak no more of rebirth and liberation. Only when the breath fades and life ends and consciousness goes to the netherworld do they begin ten recitations. This is exactly like closing the door after the thief has gone — of what use is it? The matter of birth and death is great; one must exert one's own strength. If a single thought is mistaken, one suffers for kalpas — who can take one's place? Think on this, think on this!” (Quoted from the Longshu Pure Land Text.)

blocks.text: 19. The Essential Doctrine of the Dharma-Treasure

inline.s: The essential doctrine of the Dharma-treasure: The two statements “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha” are in truth the essential doctrine of the Dharma-treasure of all the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times.

[Once the two statements of the Contemplation Sutra, “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha,” are raised, then the meanings beyond the words — “the mind not making the Buddha, the mind not being the Buddha; the mind making the nine realms, the mind being the nine realms; the mind not making the nine realms, the mind not being the nine realms” — are all made clear. Alas! If one truly understands this principle and still does not recite the Buddha's name, then there is nothing I can do with him.]

In the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, the Buddha said: “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha.” The meanings beyond the words — “this mind not making the Buddha, this mind then not being the Buddha; this mind making the nine realms, this mind then being the nine realms; this mind not making the nine realms, this mind then not being the nine realms” — are then perfectly clear. Alas! If one truly understands this principle and still does not recite the Buddha's name, then there is nothing I can do with him.

[This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha] In the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life the Buddha said: “Next you should contemplate the Buddha. Why? Because the Tathagatas of all the Buddhas are the dharmakaya realm, entering into the thoughts of all living beings. Therefore, when you living beings think of the Buddha, this mind is endowed with the thirty-two marks and the eighty secondary signs. This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha. The ocean of the Buddhas' correct and universal knowledge is born from the thought.” [Correct and universal knowledge] One of the Buddha's ten honorable titles: correct and universal knowledge, truly knowing all dharmas. [Then there is nothing I can do with him] (For such a person) I truly can do nothing with him; “none” means to have nothing.

[The two statements of the Contemplation Sutra, “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha,” are not only the essential doctrine and Dharma-essentials of that one sutra, but in truth the essential doctrine of the great Dharma of the entire teaching of Sakyamuni Tathagata's lifetime; not only the essential doctrine of the Dharma-treasure of the one Buddha Sakyamuni, but in truth the essential doctrine of the Dharma-treasure of all the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times. This doctrine once penetrated, what doctrine is not penetrated? This Dharma once made clear, what Dharma is not clear? It is the saying that though one's learning be not extensive, one may rank with the highest worthies.]

The two statements of the Sutra of the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha,” are not only the essential doctrine and Dharma-essentials of that one sutra, but in truth the essential doctrine of the great Dharma of the entire teaching of Sakyamuni Tathagata's lifetime; not only the essential doctrine of the Dharma-treasure of the one Buddha Sakyamuni, but in truth the essential doctrine of the Dharma-treasure of all the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times. This doctrine once penetrated, what doctrine is not penetrated? This Dharma once made clear, what Dharma is not clear? Therefore by firmly grasping the two statements “This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha,” and with such faith, such understanding, such practice, though one's learning be not extensive, one may reach the station of the highest worthies.
